I'm surrounded by forest. We have pretty robust volunteer fire fighter program as we are all in this together. Last year and year before we had 200+ people show up every time we had a wildfire. The county has a helicopter with a fire retardant tank, as well. BUT, if a firestorm comes my way, I want to be able to hunker down for a day in a fireproof shelter.

I am interested to see what you folks do for forest fire preparedness. I have been researching. The biggest issue I am seeing is ventilation. I have read that if you can pressurize your shelter with an o2 tank you can keep smoke out. The other way to go is filtration. There is company that specializes in above/below ground fire proof structures.

https://www.survivalcenter.com/UG.html

For an underground fire proof bunker with air filtration from these guys you are looking at around $100k. At this point, I can't really justify that expense.

So I am considering just building something myself. This wouldn't be long term. If the nukes fly I am not interested in surviving in a post apocalyptic world, anyway. I will run toward the blast. I just want to be able to breath underground and not be cooked for 24 hours. So, anybody done anything like this?
We create a hundred feet or more defensible perimeter around our house... However, we happen to be heavily surrounded by manzanitas which burn hot as fuck.

I know there's things like copper roofs and stone/brick walls that can make your house pretty fireproof. Keeping the area clean as well, as was previously mentioned. I'd feel ok inside a stone structure with a copper roof and 100 feet of clearance around me, but you're right, it's the air that would probably kill you. You're AC unit, which would most likely be outside, would either burn up, overheat or the loss of electricity would make it useless. At that point, heat's going to be a massive problem as well. The air tends to get hot around a forest fire and fires suck incredible amounts of oxygen out of the air as well. Even if you had 100 scuba tanks, the heat is still going to be a problem.
I think a 100' buffer zone would be sufficient, if they were in a basement. Most firestorms are rained out by the same storm system that starts them

They key to fireproofing a structure is pretty straightforward: routine maintenance. The main reasons a house goes up in flames is the debris and flammable plantlife around the building. Keep roofs and gutters clear of leaves and pine needles, keep plants away from the house far enough so they cant act as kindling. Keep trees far enough from the house that when they catch fire they wont fall close to the house.

There are many common building materials that are quite fire resistant and wont go up in flames just ebcause a hot ember landed on them. The goal is keep the trees far enough from the house so the house only ever has to deal with hot embers, and keep the house clear of debris so that the hot embers will not start a small fire that will engulf the entire house.

You need to learn to tend the forest as a community. Canopy fire (the dangerous type of forest fire) is a result of the forest being unhealthy. Unhealthy forest should not have lots of high bushy undergrowth. There should be mechanisms in place to prevent extensive and dense undergrowth such as the shade of mature trees, grazing animals or small brush fires.

A perimeter of grass will go a long way to protect property. Most houses usually catch fire from cinders on the roof so metal or tile roofing should be used.

Talk to elders in your community to find out if they used to do seasonal burns. It might be necessary in your location.
Look at the aussie stuff. It's a thing for them, and a lot simpler than you might imagine

You can't take out heat or air from the equation. (Air matters the most, which is why wind is a bigger predictor than dry.) You can only take away the fuel.

Clear away all the fuel from around your structure. That's your best bet. Sparks and embers can travel up to two miles, but if you have removed all the fuel for 100 yards from around your structure, just a common garden hose can wet your structure enough that embers can't get a foothold. Get rid of the trees, keep the grass mowed short, get out with a hose and a sprayer for your roof when the fire gets close, and you are as good as you are going to get.
